You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# ARC Grid Reasoning

Use for ARC-style visual/grid transformation tasks, including streams where tasks recur with fresh inputs.

## Recurring task-d2414d9a caution and this failed instance
Task d2414d9a remains unresolved. Across recurring examples, uniform background cells are selectively recolored to the embedded marker color; selection is nontrivial and NOT ordinary flood fill. In this instance we used all 8 demos and failed all 8 submissions. Test grid 22x17, background 0, marker 5 cluster near lower-right (rows 15-18, cols 13-15), distractor foreground 6. Demos (summaries):
- Pair 1, 13x26, bg4, marker5. Marker forms small irregular object around r2-6,c8-10. Output selectively recolors many 4 cells to 5 throughout grid, notably scattered regions, while leaving many similar 4 cells unchanged.
- Pair 2, 16x13,bg2,marker8: short vertical/diagonal seed near upper-right; many selected 2s changed to 8, scattered across rows 1-13, while most 2s unchanged.
- Pair 3,19x19,bg9,marker8: several marker seeds around r10-12,c7-9; many 9s changed to 8 across broad regions; most other 9s remain.
- Pair 4,18x22,bg8,marker6: seed at r1-3,c3-9, output selectively recolors 8s to 6 scattered across grid, concentrated in lower/left and some middle areas.
- Pair 5,24x10,bg0,marker2 vertical line at r2-4,c5: many 0s selectively become 2, with dense broad regions in left columns early and varying positions elsewhere; 6s and most zeros preserved.
- Pair 6,13x14,bg5,marker7: seed around r6-9,c4-8; only a small region to right/top around r4-7,c10-13 changes from 5 to 7, leaving most background unchanged.
- Pair 7,12x27,bg4,marker3: seed near upper-left (r0-2,c4-5); extensive but selective 4→3 changes broadly throughout grid, with conspicuous large untouched 4 regions.
- Pair 8,23x12,bg2,marker6: seed near r12-14,c6-8; selective 2→6 changes across upper rows and near seed/bottom, most cells unchanged.
Failed candidate families on this test: global recolor; 4-neighbor flood fill; 8-neighbor flood fill; 0-components adjacent to seed; local 3x3/8-neighbor dilation; row/column projections from seed; identity/preserve seed only. All rejected. Do not repeat these. Need derive exact geometric/relational selection using all demo changed-cell masks; likely structured relation beyond connectivity, not enough evidence here. Always compare all changed and unchanged cells; don't extrapolate from proximity or component connectivity alone.

## Recurring task-197199f9: 3x3 downsample by non-background majority
Partition into aligned 3x3 blocks; output the modal non-background color per block, ignoring the uniform canvas/background color. If a block contains only background, output background. Confirmed by two demos (18x18→6x6 and 24x24→8x8) and accepted multiple tests, including 12x12→4x4. Partition into aligned 3x3 blocks; output the modal non-background color per block, ignoring uniform canvas/background (if no foreground, output background). A further accepted 12x12 test with background 5 produced [[0,0,0,0],[3,9,0,1],[9,8,1,3],[0,9,9,0]]. Do not center-sample or top-left-sample. No tie case observed; if tied foreground colors occur, request a demo if the answer could change. 8 demo requests and 8 wrong attempts in a recurrence ended unsolved; avoid expensive center-guess repetition.

## Recurring task-648a8222: extend incomplete horizontal bars to right edge
A demo with background 8 and foreground 7 contained several horizontal runs. Only selected row-runs of 7 were extended to the right edge by recoloring the remaining cells in that row to 1: in the first example, rows 6 and 7 (0-indexed) had foreground 7 reaching to col 20, then cols 21-22 became 1. Other bars/runs remained unchanged, so selection is not simply every row containing 7; the exact selector remains uncertain. A second demo (background 0, bar color 5) showed 1 replacing only the zero-valued suffix after a bar: row 0 cols16-18; row 7 cols13-18; row 10 cols8-18. Thus extend the marked horizontal bar to the right edge for rows with an incomplete bar, changing cells after its right endpoint to 1; completed runs reaching the edge remain unchanged. On the test, the bar on row 10 (0-indexed) has 6 through col20 and background 0 in cols21-25, so recolor those five suffix cells to 1. Preserve all other rows/cells. Confirmed correct on task-648a8222 test (22x26, background 0, bar color 6).

## Recurring task-11bc55ea: shift foreground down one row
The transform is a one-row downward translation of the entire grid pattern, preserving background and foreground values and clipping the bottom row. The top row becomes background. This is repeatedly demo-confirmed: pair 1 shifted sparse 9s down (2x10); pair 2 shifted an irregular 8 shape down (9x7); pair 3 shifted an irregular 0 pattern down (9x22); pair 4 shifted 9 pattern down (3x14); pair 6 shifted 9 region down (23x17); pair 7 shifted dense 1-field down (19x30); pair 8 shifted 2 block down (4x14). Pair 5 is an identity input-output pair, so does not contradict the rule. Multiple tests accepted, including backgrounds 4/3/2. Earlier accepted examples include 15x30 bg4/fg8 and 29x27 bg3/fg9. Critical pitfall: reliably transcribe the entire test grid and mechanically shift rows; manual row transcription errors caused several rejected submissions despite the right rule. Build each output row as the exact preceding input row, plus a fresh background row at top; check H×W dimensions and row lengths programmatically. Bottom source row is clipped.

## Recurring task-648a8222 accepted test update
An instance was accepted with zero wrong attempts: 22x25 background 0, full-width color-9 bar on row 8, and partial color-9 bar on row 16 spanning cols 0-19. Change only row 16's suffix cols 20-24 to color 1; preserve the full-width row and all other cells. This confirms selected-bar right-suffix completion, but does not reveal the selection criterion across varying task layouts. A prior second-demo summary suggests some examples select multiple incomplete bars, so do not assume universally “only lowest” or “every incomplete bar”; use examples to resolve selection.

## Workflow
1. Parse dimensions, background, all non-background cells, and motifs; track coordinates consistently.
2. Request demonstrations when the rule is ambiguous. One plausible interpretation is not enough; use examples to distinguish local motifs, propagation, symmetry, and global rules.
3. Infer transformations from input-output differences. Identify changed cells and color mappings, then test candidate rules against every demo. Prefer a compact rule explaining all examples over intuition-based motif extension.
4. Apply the verified rule mechanically to the test. Preserve unchanged cells and dimensions unless evidence says otherwise; account for boundaries and overlaps.
5. Before submitting, reproduce every demo output exactly using the candidate rule. Check dimensions, row lengths, legal colors, and boundary behavior. If any demo fails, refine the hypothesis or request another demo.
6. Follow the protocol exactly: one valid action JSON per turn, on the final line. Submit only a complete grid; request a demo when further evidence is worth its cost.

## Pitfalls
- A salient multi-cell object in the test may be an instruction, seed, or unrelated element, not the rule itself. Establish its role from examples.
- Never generalize a local neighborhood mapping to every marker without checking the complete demo output. Wrong submissions consume attempts.
- Keep reasoning separate from the required response format; when the task requires one action, provide only that action.

## Validation checklist
- Candidate rule reproduces every demo exactly.
- Test output has intended dimensions and legal integer colors.
- Original non-background cells are preserved or changed only as specified.
- Boundary clipping and overlapping transformations are handled consistently.
- Final response contains exactly one action object.

# Expand input as four rotated quadrants

Use when demos show an N×N input expanded to 2N×2N, with top-left quadrant unchanged and three other quadrants being rotations of the original.

## Inference and validation
1. Identify the top-left output N×N region and compare it to the input exactly.
2. Test the other three quadrants against clockwise, counterclockwise, and 180-degree rotations of the input. Compare every cell; don't infer from corners only.
3. Validate on all demos, including asymmetric/random inputs. Small symmetric examples alone may not distinguish rotations from reflections.
4. Once confirmed, concatenate quadrants: top row blocks `[A, rot90_clockwise(A)]`; bottom row blocks `[rot90_counterclockwise(A), rot180(A)]`.
5. Check output dimensions 2N×2N and all row widths before submission.

# ARC demonstration evidence processing

## task-561fb912: additional accepted instance
A later test was accepted by recoloring two repeated 6 motifs to the color of a separate 5-cell horizontal line (color 3). The repeated forms were upper-left r0 c6-8 plus r1 c7-8, and lower-right r14 c17-19 plus r15 c18-19. Both copies changed from 6 to 3; all other cells were preserved. An identity-like submission retaining them as 6 was rejected; changing both motifs to 3 was accepted. This is instance-specific evidence, not a universal task-ID rule: other examples under this ID show unrelated sparse recolorings. Seek repeated motifs and a corresponding line/object cue; do not globally recolor components.

## Recurrence: task-dff20308 — unresolved instance review (8 demos, 8 failed submissions)

Do not treat any earlier simple ray/marker interpretation below as established; the current task recurrence failed its complete attempt budget. Current test (25x16): bg5; top edge color2 row0 cols3-8; bottom edge color2 row24 cols10-15; color6 markers (6,7),(15,8),(21,5),(21,6). Eight test submissions were rejected. Failed candidate families included: full horizontal/vertical rays from every marker with marker→4; rectangle between marker extrema; row/column projections from edge bars; only adjacent-marker fill; marker recoloring only; marker-column shafts; one-direction rays toward the nearest bar. None should be reused as a validated rule.

Current instance demo constraints:
- Demo1 (24x17 bg2, edge bars color8 at top-left cols0-6 and bottom cols7-13; markers 0 at (10,12),(15,10),(20,13)): output contains selected 0-filled vertical/horizontal tracks, some markers become4, but several same-color candidates remain unchanged. The visible output: columns3 and5-6 are filled 0 down rows1-23; col12 gets 0 from row11 downward with seed at (10,12) changed4; col10 gets 0 from row16 down with seed (15,10) changed4; col13 gets 0 rows21-22 with seed at (20,13) changed4. Edge bars preserved.
- Demo2 (6x29 bg3; top bar color1 cols16-24; bottom bar color1 cols0-8; 7 markers at (2,20),(2,21),(3,19)): output paints 7 in rectangular-like strips at cols3-5 and col8 rows0-5, plus cols19-21/24 rows0-1; marker group converts to4 at (2,20),(2,21),(3,19) with some adjacent 7 retained. Highly selective; no simple global rays.
- Demo3 (24x29 bg0; left bar color7 rows7-11, right bar color7 rows19-23; 6 markers at (7,14),(9,21),(10,22),(11,10)): color6 rays/segments fill rows7,9-11 from left boundary up to selected marker(s), with marker→4; full bottom rows19,21-23 are filled 6 across interior cols0-27, while row20 remains untouched. Edge 7 preserved. Selection is not every marker row.
- Demo4 (22x29 bg5; top bar color6 cols5-13; bottom bar color6 cols20-28; 0 markers at (8,8),(14,13),(17,10)): output writes 0 vertical tracks at cols8,10,13,23,25,28 with a patterned selection; markers become4, but not all possible marker rows/columns are filled. Bars preserved.
- Demo5 (14x6 bg0; right vertical bar8 rows8-10, left bar8 rows11-13; 3 markers (9,3),(10,1)): marker cells→4; output fills 3 at row9 col4, row10 cols2-4, and rows12-13 cols1-5. Selective region/edge-driven extension.
- Demo6 (30x8 bg8; right bar3 rows0-10, left bar3 rows11-21; 5 markers assorted rows11-21): rows0-10 interior cols0-6 entirely recolored5; rows11-21 cols1-6 entirely5 except original 8 cells to right of individual markers in rows with markers; all marker seeds→4. Edge bars remain3. Pattern depends on marker distribution and edge-bar framing.
- Demo7 (16x25 bg3; top-left bar0 row0 cols0-8, bottom bar0 row15 cols10-18; 2 markers at row4 cols12,17; row5 col13; row7 cols10,15; row9 col14; row10 col11; row12 col18): output fills large left region with color2 cols0-5 and cols7-8 rows1-14, retaining col6 as 3; separately makes varied 2 regions around marker fields in cols10-17; all selected marker cells become4. Exact selector complex.
- Demo8 (8x5 bg8; top row zeros c2-3, bottom row zeros c0-1, 6 marker at (6,3)): output adds 6 in col1 rows0-6 and col3 rows1-5, converts marker (6,3)→4; preserves edge zeros and other cells. This disproves simplistic “extend marker both axes” as universal.

Shared robust observation: some interior marker-color cells are recolored4, and edge-bar color is generally preserved. However, even the set of markers selected for 4 and the fill geometry vary; the rule remains unresolved. If this ID recurs, first reconstruct all demo diffs and discover the selection predicate/encoding; do not repeat previous broad ray hypotheses or blindly submit. Requests cost a demo each; synthesize every pair before the next action. Keep one valid JSON action per turn.

## Recurrence: task-b39d719b — confirmed transformation

Tile input grid A into a 2×2 arrangement of A and its 90° clockwise, 90° counterclockwise, and 180° rotations, respectively: top-left=A, top-right=CW(A), bottom-left=CCW(A), bottom-right=180°(A). For an N×N grid, output is 2N×2N, each quadrant N×N. Demo pair: 9×9 input produced 18×18 output; top-left reproduced the input exactly, while other quadrants matched the corresponding rotations. The all-5 11×11 test therefore becomes a 22×22 grid of 5s in all four quadrants; accepted. Uniform inputs do not distinguish rotation orientation, but the asymmetric demo supports the quadrant ordering. Do not confuse this with 2× nearest-neighbor cell expansion.

## Earlier claimed ray recurrence (superseded/unvalidated)

IMPORTANT: The later task-dff20308 instance above used all 8 submissions and rejected every one. This prior three-demo/accepted-test note pertains to a different occurrence and must not be generalized; current exact selector remains unresolved.

An earlier note claimed a simple universal rule: edge bars project marker-colored rays and markers change to4. This was directly falsified by eight wrong submissions in a later/current instance; do not rely on it.

Confirmed by three demos and an accepted test.

- A uniform background grid may contain paired edge bars (color 2) along a row or column, plus isolated interior marker(s) (often color 5). Edge bars project the other color (the color of isolated markers) inward along their row/column; each interior marker extends in both directions on its own row and column.
- In demo 1 (16x21), vertical edge bars of color 2 at right edge rows 0-4 and left edge rows 11-15 align to project horizontal 1-rays on rows 0 and 11. A lone 1 at (0,1) was recolored 4, and projection filled row 0 from col 2 through 19 and row 11 from col 1 through 20.
- In demo 2 (10x24), horizontal edge bars color 8 at left rows 0-1 and right rows 8-9. The isolated 0 at (8,4) was recolored 4; row 0 filled with 0 from col 1 through 23, and row 8 filled 0 from col 5 through 22, preserving edge bars.
- In demo 3 (17x6), horizontal edge bars of color 2 at top cols 4-5 and bottom cols 2-3 project vertical 5-rays down column 4 (rows 1-16), and up column 3 (rows 0-15), preserving bars. The isolated 5 at (9,2) changed to 4; its column extended with 5 both directions (rows 0-8, 10-15).
- Accepted test (14x18): background 8, edge bars color 2: top-right row 0 cols 16-17 and bottom row 13 cols 5-6; interior 5 markers at (2,6) and (6,5). Project 5-rays from edge bars along their rows/columns: row 0 bar doesn't produce visible 5 into left because bars at right; wait accepted output only had col 16-17 5 filled downward rows 1-13, and row 13 5 filled from col 7-17. Extend each marker's row and column in both directions in color 5, recoloring each marker itself to 4. The marker at (2,6) made col 6 rows 0-13 5, then marker is 4; the marker at (6,5) made row 6 cols 0-17 5 and col 5 rows 0-5 and 7-12 5, with marker 4. At crossing (6,6), 5 remains. Preserve background elsewhere and original edge bars.

Important: edge-bar rays use the color of the isolated markers; isolated markers change to 4 and emit orthogonal rays. Reproduce the three demo masks and accepted test exactly. The prior session note saying the task remained unresolved is superseded by this accepted recurrence; avoid its speculative final output.


## Workflow
1. Extract dimensions, background and non-background coordinates, exact input/output differences, and conspicuously unchanged regions.
2. State the concrete constraint this pair establishes: color roles, selection, direction, endpoints, phase, preservation, or boundaries. Do not infer beyond the data.
3. Compare it against every earlier pair. Identify which candidate rules survive or are contradicted, and what predictions differ on the test.
4. Before requesting another pair, name the unresolved ambiguity and explain how its answers could change the test prediction. If the latest pair has not been analyzed, analyze it first.
5. Submit only when a candidate reproduces all available demos cell-by-cell. If materially different candidates remain, request a targeted pair rather than guessing.
6. In constrained ARC streams, return exactly one protocol-compliant action JSON object per turn.

## Pitfalls
- Do not spend consecutive demo requests without synthesizing the latest returned pair first.

2. State what the new pair proves and compare it against every previous pair before requesting another demo or submitting.
3. Keep a small explicit hypothesis set. For band-like or sparse stripe seeds, distinguish partial-row extension to an edge, completion of an exceptional row in a repeated pattern, motif copying, and periodic-field completion. Treat unchanged counterpart rows/cells as negative evidence.
4. Request a demo only when a specific outcome would distinguish live hypotheses and could change the test prediction. Do not request merely because more examples are available or visual structure differs.
5. Replay the leading rule against every complete demo, including boundaries and unchanged cells. Apply mechanically to the test only when all changes and non-changes are explained.
6. In protocol-constrained ARC, emit exactly one action JSON per turn.

- A visually salient seed does not explain broad output changes by itself.

Output dimensions are 3H × 2W. Form horizontal paired rows as `reverse(source_row) + source_row`. # Separator-panel transformation reasoning

Use when a full row or column separates ARC panels and output is panel-sized or a transformed mask. This is a class workflow, not a presumed crop rule.

## Workflow
1. Locate the separator; determine panel dimensions and verify output dimensions/orientation.
2. For every output coordinate, tabulate `(panel A value, panel B value, output value)`. Determine whether output derives from A, B, both, or global structure; output dimensions alone do not identify the source panel.
3. Count colors and propose foreground/background roles, but test alternatives. The most frequent color is not automatically background, nor is a sparse color automatically the selected mask.
4. Test cellwise relations: equality to either panel's foreground/background, intersections, differences, palette remapping, and direct masks. Record unchanged matching cells as counterexamples.
5. Separate spatial selection from palette mapping. A rule may select cells in one panel by comparison with the other, then map selected and unselected cells separately.
6. Implement the candidate and reproduce every demo exactly: dimensions, every output color, and unchanged cells. Visual agreement on a subset is insufficient.
7. On rejection, discard the entire candidate mapping. Do not repeat it or submit a small variation without new discriminating evidence.
8. Request a demo only after naming which live hypotheses it separates and how outcomes change the test prediction. Synthesize each returned pair before requesting again.

- A matching output shape does not prove the corresponding input panel supplies the output.

# ARC demonstration budget discipline

Use alongside general ARC grid reasoning when demonstrations are costly or capped.

## Workflow
1. After each pair, identify the exact proposition it establishes: color role, anchor, orientation, selection criterion, changed-cell rule, boundary behavior, or transformation class.
2. Compare the new pair with all previous pairs jointly. Separate genuinely new constraints from visual novelty; different colors or seed layouts may encode the same operation.
3. Keep a short list of live hypotheses and the specific evidence that distinguishes them. Request another pair only if its possible outcomes could separate those hypotheses and change the output.

5. After several heterogeneous examples, pause to synthesize the shared operation and test it mechanically against all pairs. Check whether a general spatial rule explains them before fixating on an intuitive motif.
6. Once the evidence supports a rule, replay it cell-by-cell on every demo and apply it to the test. Near the cap, prefer the best-supported candidate over an uninformative request.

- Repeated requests without a discriminating question spend budget without improving inference.

# Infer periodic ARC grid fields

Use for ARC examples where rows or columns shift cyclically, diagonal stripes appear, or a triangular seed may encode a full periodic field.

## Workflow
1. Record input/output changes as coordinates and input→output colors; identify which input cells are preserved versus filled.
2. Check whether equal-shift rows/columns repeat and whether colors advance along diagonals.
3. Infer the shortest color cycle, grid period, and phase from multiple rows/columns; do not infer continuation solely from the seed's visible shape.
4. Apply the candidate rule over the complete output and verify every demo cell, including boundaries and regions far from the seed.
5. For the test grid, apply the verified period and phase mechanically. Confirm shape and color legality.

## Demonstration cost discipline
Request another example only when it distinguishes concrete competing rules or resolves phase/boundary ambiguity. Each request consumes score; avoid redundant demos once the periodic rule is determined. Never submit a formula based only on a seed-shaped subset: reproduce every output cell in every demo first. If examples support distinct formats (uniform horizontal bands versus diagonal seed), infer the representation from the current task's actual input. Distinguish a fixed color cycle by rows from a two-dimensional modular field; do not carry the latter into a full-width-band task.

## Pitfalls
- A diagonal or triangular arrangement may be a partial encoding of a 2D periodic field, not a motif to copy.
- Period alone is insufficient: a phase offset can produce a plausible but wrong field.
- Do not extrapolate a visually compelling pattern until it reproduces all observed output cells.
- Keep the protocol response to the single JSON action required by the puzzle.

# ARC object-relation audit

Use this class-level checklist when a grid contains distinct objects in multiple colors, sparse singleton cells, or examples whose changed object is not obvious.

## Workflow
1. Segment non-background cells into objects/components; record each object's color, bounding box, shape, and singleton/line status.
2. Compare every demo input and output cellwise. Record changed cells and which object(s) changed; explicitly record conspicuously unchanged objects as negative evidence.
3. Test relational hypotheses before local shape-copy hypotheses: a marker may encode a target color or select an object by color, shape, adjacency, or position. Check whether the same relation predicts the changed object across demos with different palettes and layouts.
4. State competing hypotheses and the test prediction each implies. Request another demo only if a specific outcome discriminates them and could change the prediction.
5. Verify the complete predicted output, preserving all untouched cells and objects, before submission.

## Recurrence: task-561fb912 (mixed demos; previous solves unresolved)

### Confirmed rule from an additional solved instance
In one instance, a partially occluded/irregular `6` motif occurred twice: a 3-cell horizontal bar at the upper-left and a 3-cell horizontal bar at the lower-right, with corresponding second-row shape pieces. Both were changed to the same color as the separate horizontal 5-cell line (color 3); other objects remained unchanged. Input details: rows 0–1 near cols 6–8 had 6s (`row0 c6-8`, `row1 c7-8`); rows 14–15 near cols 17–19 had 6s (`r14 c17-19`, `r15 c18-19`). Output changed these 6s to 3, retaining all else. The first submitted identity-like grid was rejected because it kept the target shapes as 6. The corrected output recolored those motif cells to 3 and was accepted.

This supports a relation in that instance: recolor the repeated motif matching the color-3 line object's pattern/role to color 3, while preserving unrelated shapes. It is not a general task-wide rule; earlier examples had assorted sparse recolorings. For future recurrences, carefully compare repeated/related objects with line or shape cues; do not blindly map every component or assume color mapping without demo support.

## Recurrence: task-561fb912 (mixed demos; previous solves unresolved)
This task family is sparse selective recoloring amidst noisy multicolor shapes and line/corner markers. The selection criterion may depend on larger structures; do not guess by source color or component size. Historical examples were inconsistent and insufficient to establish one general rule. One prior instance was accepted after recoloring selected broad bar-shaped objects based on a 1D geometric relationship; another remained unsolved. Treat demonstrations as evidence to build a task-specific predicate, not a fixed mapping.

- horizontal 4-cell segment at row 5, columns 7-10 (0-based indexing);

The accepted output recolored the color-6 horizontal bar immediately adjacent/parallel to the long color-5 horizontal bar (the demo context suggests selecting an object aligned with / matching long-bar shape cues), while leaving other 6 components untouched. It also changed nearby color-6 shapes to 5 as explicitly encoded in accepted grid. Exact accepted cells: row5 c7-10; row6 c7,c9,c10; row7 c9,c10. Do not overgeneralize this without validating demos; prior recurrence confirms uncertainty.

Current session demos (8) and outputs: demo1 changed only a vertical 4-cell component of color 8 at rows 11-14? to 3; demo2 changed a 2x2-ish color-7 component at top-left to 5; demo3 changed a two-cell color-2 vertical component to 5; demo4 changed a 2x2 color-3 object to 7; demo5 changed a bottom-center color-3 component to 9; demo6 changed a lower-left color-3 component to 8; demo7 changed the lower color-5 silhouette to 0; demo8 changed two color-9 cells to 3. These only establish sparse recolorings, not a reliable universal selection rule.

Operational rule: preserve all else; replay full demos and detect any common geometric relation before reusing. Avoid serial demo requests without synthesis.

## Pitfalls

Use alongside ARC reasoning when each response must contain exactly one JSON action.

# Recurring separator-panel analysis

Use alongside `arc-panel-relations` and `arc-demo-recovery` when a separator-panel task recurs but prior examples or feedback do not establish a stable mapping.

## Workflow
1. Split at the full separator; verify both panel dimensions and output panel orientation.
2. For every example, record each coordinate as `(left, right, output)` and identify output base color, exception colors, and every exception coordinate.
3. Test explicit predicates separately: intersection, union, equality, one-sided marker, ordered pair, and panel-background conditions. Audit negative evidence: candidate cells that do not change are as important as matches.
4. Track palette mapping separately from selection. A correct mask with the wrong base or exception palette is still incorrect.
5. Reconcile all demos before submitting. If examples appear to use different predicates, do not force a universal rule from a few coincident cells; request a demo only if outcomes resolve a specific test-relevant ambiguity.
6. After rejection, invalidate the whole candidate and avoid near-variants without new evidence.
7. In constrained ARC turns, output exactly one legal JSON action on the final line. Do not let tool commentary or delegation displace the action; keep delegation bounded and synthesize results directly.

## Pitfalls
- Output dimensions do not identify which panel supplies the base color.
- Shared markers may explain some exceptions but not all; verify the entire mask.
- A new example may contradict a plausible earlier pattern. Preserve uncertainty instead of encoding an unvalidated rule as solved.
- Repeated tool calls or agents are not progress unless they add exact cellwise evidence.

# Infer periodic ARC fields

Use for ARC examples where horizontal/vertical bands, diagonal marks, or triangular seeds may encode a complete periodic color field.

## Workflow
1. Record seed coordinates, colors, and output differences. Determine whether seed cells are preserved, expanded, or used only to encode a field.
2. Compare equal-shift rows and columns; test whether output colors vary by row, column, or both.
3. Infer the shortest cycle and exact phase from all demonstrations. For mixed examples, full-width bands may reveal the color cycle while a diagonal seed establishes that output phase depends on both coordinates.
4. Test compact modular candidates such as `cycle[(a*r+b*c+k) mod p]` against every output cell, especially the origin, boundaries, and positions distant from the seed. Reject any candidate that mismatches even one cell.
5. Apply only the fully verified formula mechanically to the test dimensions and check row widths and legal colors.

## Recurrence: task-64b74fc5 (FAILED; 8 demos, 8 wrong submissions; do not reuse guesses)

- Pair 2 27x27: input bands rows8=3,19=9,20=8,21=3,22=8; output sequence begins [8,3,8,3,9,8,3,8,3,9,...] and repeats, with 3-cycle pattern interrupted by 9 every 5th row.
- Pair 3 10x10: diagonal seeds; output is a repeating 7-color periodic field with diagonals, confirming some diagonal-to-field behavior in that example.
- Pair 4 23x23: bands row1=6,row15=3,row20=8; output rows repeat [3,6,8] from row0.
- Pair 5 15x15: diagonal color9/4 seeds; output checkerboard 9/4, i.e. output[r,c]=9 if (r+c)%2==0 else 4.
- Pair 6 28x28: horizontal seeds row1=9,row7=9,row9=7,row11=5,row12=6,row15=5,row17=5,row22=5,row23=8. Output row sequence period 16 starting [7,9,5,6,5,8,5,9,5,7,9,5,6,5,8,5] and repeats/clips.
- Pair 7 5x5: input rows of a diagonal period sequence; output differs only select zeros replaced with 8 and zeros at other cells with 5; rule not confidently inferred.
- Pair 8 26x26: bands: r5=9,r6=7,r8=2,r11-12=9,r18=1,r19=2,r22=2,r25=7. Output has complex row periodic sequence, e.g. first rows [1,2,9,9,2,9,7,7,2,1,2,9,9,2,9,7,7,2,1,2,9,9,2,9,7,7], period-like 18.

`[[0,7,0,5,6,0,0,8,0],[7,0,5,6,0,0,8,0,0],[0,5,6,0,0,8,0,0,7],[5,6,0,0,8,0,0,7,0],[6,0,0,8,0,0,7,0,0],[0,0,8,0,0,7,0,0,1],[0,8,0,0,7,0,0,1,8],[8,0,0,7,0,0,1,8,0],[0,0,7,0,0,1,8,0,8]]`.

Pair 4: 18x18 multi-diagonal/color seed produced 2D periodic rows with period 6; first six rows [3,6,7,3,2,7], [6,7,3,2,7,3], [7,3,2,7,3,6], [3,2,7,3,6,7], [2,7,3,6,7,3], [7,3,6,7,3,2]. All eight test submissions failed. Several were accidental identity copies (same submitted input repeated), while others tried replacing color-1 diagonal with 5, or row/diagonal cycles based on visible input colors. No candidate was confirmed. Do not transfer a cycle from any unrelated demo. Crucially, input test itself contains repeated structured diagonals and may encode a 2D modular field; derive the exact cycle and mapping from seed coordinates/colors, then verify all seed cells. This recurrence remains unresolved; avoid claiming any formula as established.
An earlier distinct instance used a 19x19 diagonal seed and was solved with a period-3 field. This is not evidence that the later failed 7x7 uniform-band test should use that output formula. Keep instances and evidence separate.


The transformation fills the entire grid with the 2D periodic field indicated by the diagonal and nearby color-pattern seeds. For this instance the rule is `output[r][c] = cycle[(r-c) mod 3]` with cycle indexed `[2,6,6]` (equivalently output 2 iff `(r-c) mod 3 == 0`, else 6). This reproduces the test and was confirmed correct after two rejected candidates.

Demo: 19x19 input had a short descending diagonal of color 1 near the upper-right and a diagonal arrangement of 8s in bottom-left. Output repeated a 3-color checker-like field: row 0 begins `[1,8,8,1,8,8,...]`, row 1 `[8,1,8,8,1,8,...]`, row 2 `[8,8,1,8,8,1,...]`. Thus output is `cycle[(r+c) mod 3]` with cycle `[1,8,8]`; note demo orientation differs from test's descending diagonal/color phase. Treat it as evidence for diagonal periodic fields, but derive coefficients and phase from the actual test seeds rather than transferring a formula blindly.

Two test submissions using the opposite orientation / row pattern were rejected. Correct test rows obey `(r-c) mod 3`: for r=0, colors are `[6,6,2]` repeating; r=1 begins `[2,6,6]`; r=2 begins `[6,2,6]`. Input's 2 diagonal at coordinates `(r,c)=(0,2),(1,3),...` aligns with phase `r-c == -2 mod 3 == 1`; input 6s on neighboring diagonal reinforce remaining two phases. A robust solving procedure: map each seed color to its residue class, infer the complete period and coordinate linear form, then fill all cells; verify the seed values before submitting.

Important: same task family may use different orientation/phase according to seed. Do not reuse the demo's `r+c` formula blindly. Use seed coordinate differences to determine whether field depends on `r+c`, `r-c`, or another modular linear combination. Validate every seed cell and grid dimension. Protocol requires one JSON action only.

## Pitfalls
- A stripe-only example can make a row-cycle appear plausible even when another seed form reveals a 2D diagonal field.
- Period without phase is insufficient; an offset can make the entire output wrong.
- Do not extrapolate from the visible seed sequence without reproducing the full demo output cell-by-cell.

# Fill gaps between aligned markers

In ARC grids with a uniform background and scattered markers, check whether every open interval between consecutive markers in the same row or column is recolored (often with a third color). Task task-3da70d3c confirms the row-only rule on a test: background 3, marker 5, fill 2. Recurring task task-3da70d3c is confirmed: recolor only cells strictly between consecutive marker-8 cells in each row with color 2, preserving marker endpoints and all other cells. This holds across varied backgrounds and marker colors; establish actual colors from current input/demos. Another demo: background 1, marker 4, fill 2, likewise row-only. Do not assume marker color 8 or 5. The 18x24 test with background 4 and marker 8 solved by this rule. Do not fill vertical gaps or extend beyond endpoints. The 13x17 test with background 8 and marker 0 confirmed the same rule, including rows with adjacent marker pairs, one-marker/no-marker rows, and separated multiple pairs. The 17x13 test validated multiple markers, single gaps, and rows with zero/one marker. For each row, recolor only cells strictly between consecutive horizontal markers; preserve marker endpoints and all other cells. Confirm colors from task evidence rather than assuming they transfer to unrelated tasks. An older task-2070c748 remains unresolved and should not be conflated with this confirmed task.

## Procedure
1. Identify the background, marker color, and replacement fill color from demonstrations.
2. For each row, list marker columns in increasing order. Fill only the cells strictly between each consecutive pair; preserve marker endpoints and all cells beyond the outermost markers.
3. Apply only the horizontal intervals unless a demonstration explicitly confirms vertical filling. Preserve original markers and background cells outside these intervals. A pair separated by exactly one cell still colors that single intervening cell.
4. Validate which axes transform from the demos; never assume the operation is symmetric across rows and columns.
5. Validate against all demonstrations, including cases with no aligned pair, adjacent markers, multiple markers on one line, and overlaps.

## Pitfall
Do not extend a marker-to-marker interval past its endpoints, and do not fill entire rows or columns. The rule applies to consecutive aligned marker pairs; endpoints remain unchanged.

## Example
Markers at row positions 1, 2, and 6 preserve those cells and fill the open interval at positions 3–5. The same operation applies vertically; overlapping horizontal and vertical intervals simply form a union.

# Task 1a8d9993: strict interior fill, preserve perimeter

A solved instance had background 1, rectangular frame color 9, and a one-cell defect within its strict interior. The correct output changed only the interior hole from 1 to 4; the perimeter and all exterior cells were unchanged.

## Coordinate evidence
In the 26x12 test, the frame's row extent was 3–5 and column extent 1–9 (1-indexed). The cell at row 4, column 8 lies on the frame row and remained 1; recoloring it to 4 was the first incorrect submission. The accepted output recolored row 5, column 8 (strict interior) to 4. This demonstrates that apparent frame gaps should not be mistaken for interior fill targets.

## Additional accepted instance (2026-10-21): simple complete rectangle
Test input was 9x23 with background 0 and frame color 2. A 4x4 outlined frame occupied rows 1–5? More precisely, the accepted fill changed only rows 2–4, columns 4–5 (0-indexed) to 4. The frame was at rows 1–5 and columns 3–6 in zero-based coordinates, except the top edge is partially disrupted by a protruding 2 at row 2, columns 0–3; strict rectangular interior is rows 2–4, columns 4–5. All frame and exterior cells were preserved. The first submission was rejected as an invalid ARC grid due to malformed dimensions (one row had an incorrect length); the corrected 9x23 grid with those six interior cells set to 4 was accepted.

This adds a reminder: before submitting, verify every row has the exact input width (especially long grids), and fill only the strict interior of the identifiable rectangular outline. The protruding horizontal segment at row 2 was exterior and remained unchanged.

## Additional accepted instance (2026-10-21): disconnected outlined rectangles
Input was 23x9, background 7, frame color 9. The first accepted submission mistakenly filled enclosed 7-cells with 4, but missed cells that were already 7 in the strict interiors and did not change those to 4. The correct output fills every strict-interior cell of the qualifying rectangles, regardless of its input color, to 4.

The top 4x4 outlined rectangle occupies rows 0–3, columns 1–4; its strict interior is rows 1–2, columns 2–3, all set to 4. The next 6x4 rectangle occupies rows 5–10, columns 2–5; its strict interior is rows 6–9, columns 3–4, all set to 4. Do not fill the lower vertical line at column 3 below row 10: it is not a closed rectangle. Preserve the boundary, including irregular exterior protrusions, and all cells outside strict interiors.

This instance resolves an important ambiguity: interior fill is unconditional across colors (here both background 7 and 9-valued cells became 4); it is not merely recoloring background cells. Identify closed rectangular outlines, then recolor every coordinate strictly between their outer boundary rows and columns.

## Procedure
1. Identify each enclosing rectangular frame and its boundary coordinates; the puzzle may contain multiple frames.
2. Exclude all frame cells, including any background-colored gaps in a boundary row/column.
3. For the confirmed 3x3 incomplete-square pattern, fill the *vertical enclosed channel*: the strict interior is the column between the two side posts, over rows strictly between top and bottom caps **and also intervening rows where the bottom cap is interrupted by a horizontal extension**. Do not assume the horizontal extension defines a topological rectangle boundary. On this task's tested pattern, fill all background cells between the two side posts from immediately below the top cap through immediately above the bottom cap, to 4; preserve all 9 frame/extension cells and exterior.
4. Check dimensions and every changed coordinate before submitting.

Test 25x12, background 6, structure color 9. The visible motif has a 3-wide top cap at row 18, side posts at columns 2 and 4 (0-indexed), and a bottom cap at row 24. A long horizontal 9-extension crosses row 21, extending left and right from the left side post, with a gap at column 3. This is supported by demo 1: background 5, structure 2; a pair of side posts with interrupted horizontal material along a row, and the target interior was filled only in the two-cell-wide channel between side boundaries, including the gap row. The rule is not simply flood-fill a closed rectangle or fill only cells strictly between intact top/bottom horizontal edges: recognize the vertical channel bounded by the side posts, fill its interior regardless of a crossing/open horizontal extension, and preserve structure-colored cells.

A prior submission that filled only rows 19–20 and 22–23 (excluding the gap at the horizontal-extension row 21) was rejected. The accepted output filled rows 19–23 at the central column. This evidence sharpens the rule: fill every background cell in the channel between vertical posts, including the background gap in a crossing extension.

## Additional instance evidence (2026-10-21)

# ARC Rejected-Hypothesis Discipline

Use after feedback says an ARC submission is incorrect, especially when the demo budget is exhausted or only a few attempts remain.

## Recovery sequence
1. Record the submitted grid's exact changed-cell pattern: coordinates/regions, colors, direction, and preserved cells. Label the entire hypothesis rejected, not just one color choice.
2. Re-extract all demo input/output differences, including negative evidence: unchanged rows, gaps in regular fills, boundary behavior, and unchanged markers. Keep a compact hypothesis table noting which demos falsify each candidate.
3. Before another submission, require a candidate rule to account for every demonstrated change and unchanged region. Mechanically replay it against each full demo when available; verbal resemblance is not validation.
4. Do not retry a rejected candidate with only a superficial color, axis, or extent tweak unless new evidence supports that change and resolves the prior mismatch. Prefer a materially distinct hypothesis grounded in demo evidence.
5. Spend remaining demos only on a named ambiguity whose possible outcomes would change the test prediction. Once demos are exhausted, use rejection evidence to eliminate candidates rather than repeating them.
6. In protocol-constrained puzzles, return exactly one valid action object per response and ensure submitted grid dimensions and values match the protocol.

## Bound analysis and delegation
- Tool calls should advance concrete evidence-gathering or validation. Do not repeatedly delegate the same unresolved question or spawn batches of near-duplicate agents.
- If one independent check can catch a blind spot, delegate a single focused question with precise evidence and desired result; synthesize it once, then decide.
- If uncertainty remains, make one evidence-based attempt rather than spending the response on process commentary that violates the action protocol.

## Pitfalls
- Repeating a whole-region fill after rejection is not recovery.
- A locally plausible ray or marker recoloring may explain only a few cells while missing the actual global structure.
- More analysis volume does not substitute for extracting exact differences and falsifying candidates.
- Never claim a candidate is demo-validated unless it reproduces all available examples cell by cell.

# Copy an anchored motif onto markers

When a grid contains multiple isolated marker cells plus one nearby example motif, compare motif placement to marker locations. The motif may be defined relative to a specific anchor cell within its bounding box, not its top-left.

## Procedure
1. Identify background, marker color, and the demonstrated motif's non-background cells.
2. Inspect for a seeded motif composed of a colored 3×3 patch plus a single extra same-color cell (a 3×4 or 4×3 L-like shape). Demos may show the patch duplicated by translating to each isolated marker location.
3. When isolated markers match exactly one patch cell color in the seed, infer translation by the marker-to-seed correspondence, preserving the seed's internal shape and orientation; only apply if verified by demos. The aligned seed cell need not be the motif center: task-01dcdfcb was confirmed with each marker aligned to the motif's upper-left cell.
4. Distinguish output growth from literal stamp copying: outputs can show full patch blocks surrounding each marker plus extensions. Compare demo input/output at coordinates to infer whether markers become patch anchor positions, and preserve background/other colors.

2. Find the motif's anchor by locating the marker-like cell within the motif or testing relative placements across all isolated markers.
3. For every marker, translate the motif by matching its anchor coordinate to the marker coordinate; preserve the exact offsets and colors.
4. Keep background cells unchanged; overlay motif cells at each translated position, clipping only at grid edges.
5. Preserve the original demonstrated motif if needed. Check overlaps and boundaries explicitly.

# task-647084a7: selective cleanup — unresolved exact rule

## When to Use
Use when task-647084a7 recurs with a noisy grid containing solid objects and scattered singleton markers.

## Evidence from seven demo pairs
All examples contain a uniform background, solid multi-cell blobs/rectangles, and scattered singleton noise in other colors; some blobs have foreign-color intrusions. Demonstrated outputs generally erase singleton noise and repair intrusions, while preserving genuine multi-cell objects. Cases included:
- Demo 1 bg1: remove isolated 0/3/9/5 and repair color-4 blocks; preserve color-2/8 structures.
- Demo 2 bg0: erase speckles; keep 9, 6, and 8 objects, repair noisy holes including 2x2 8.
- Demo 3 bg8: all noise erased; retain one color-5 4x7 rectangle, fill its noisy cells.
- Demo 4 bg7: remove singletons; retain 3 2x7 and 8 6x7/5x6 blocks, repair embedded color4.
- Demo 5 bg0: retain and repair color7, 9, and 3 structures; discard singleton color1 markers; repair intrusion in 9.
- Demo 6 bg4: erase isolated 0/3/9; retain/repair larger color-1 and color-0 structures.
- Demo 7 bg2: remove isolated 4s, keep two color-7 blobs and color-6 rectangle; fill holes in 7 objects.

## Test outcome and current-instance evidence
Earlier recurrence: five test submissions failed; the sixth was accepted. Acceptance alone did not establish an exact reusable predicate.

Latest full instance (8 demos, 8 submissions failed): the input had many large solid/near-solid regions of multiple colors (notably 2, 4, 5) embedded with single-cell noises and intrusions, plus other distinct multi-cell objects. Do NOT reuse any of the submitted outputs or assumptions below; all were rejected. Guesses included: clear isolated markers and repair holes in broad regions; complete selected rectangles/blocks; restore only major regions while deleting foreign colors; preserve all original speckles; combinations of marker removal and broad block completion. None solved it.

Demo evidence from latest instance (use as additional examples, but selection rule remains unresolved):
- Pair 1 (22x11, bg9): retained/fixed 0 rectangle (rows1-7, cols4-9); retained 3 block at rows12-15, cols8-10; retained 0 block at rows14-20, cols3-4. Deleted intruding 4,8,6,5,1,2 singletons and removed two 8s interrupting the 0 block; other speckles disappeared.
- Pair 2 (10x11,bg3): kept 6 3x3 and 8 blocks; removed stray 2/7s; repaired holes in selected 6 and 8 blocks, but note at least one embedded 2 was removed.
- Pair 3 (12x17,bg9): retained 7 block (r0-5,c2-5), 7 pattern at r3-7,c7-8, and 0 blocks r5-9,c11-15; removed sparse noise. Notably did NOT fill the gap between adjacent 7 structures.
- Pair 4 (12x29,bg3): repaired 4 rectangle r4-7,c7-11, 9 rectangle r3-7,c20-23, and 9 rectangle r5-10,c0-4; removed sparse noise. Other 4 regions/isolates were partly untouched (selection not just rectangle completion).
- Pair 5 (27x13,bg7): repaired 0 block r0-2,c8-12; 6 block r5-6,c5-10; 8 block r11-16,c7-12; 9 objects and bottom 0 block (r24-26,c2-6), plus 9 block at r9-10,c3-4 were retained; noise cleared. Several small areas not repaired, e.g. lower-left 9 block had one 3 intruder removed.
- Pair 6 (11x30,bg4): many 7 and 4 structures retained; removed sparse noise. Repaired 7 blocks at r4-5,c7-13 and r6-7,c18-23, preserving other complete/unmarked 7 blocks. Did not universally delete every non-4 singleton-looking pixel if part of region.
- Pair 7 (28x20,bg0): many distinct regions retained (9,5,3,7,8,1); sparse noise removed and embedded intrusions repaired. Large 5 regions on top-right/right-middle repaired with some exceptions: shape and area/selection matter. 9 rectangles expanded/repaired; some narrow 9 shapes kept unchanged. 3/7/8/1 blocks preserved and noise corrected.
- Pair 8 (26x29,bg3): repaired many broad regions: 5 at top-left and top-right; 9 blocks (e.g. r3-6,c8-12; r3-6,c21-22; r13-17,c3-8; r17-22,c13-15); 1 blocks in several regions; 5 region r10-11,c3-9 and r20-25,c6-9. Removed speckles, repaired intrusions. Yet similar objects were not all altered uniformly.

No exact object-selection criterion emerges from these summaries. Distinguish components, original shape/area, embedded intrusions, and spatial/relational cues; compare every changed AND unchanged cell. The prior generic theories (singleton deletion, rectangle fill, preserving large regions) were rejected as test prediction generators. This recurrence remains unresolved; use an evidence-led independent rule and demos if task recurs, do not copy any failed submission.


## Confirmed rule from latest recurrence
A new demo (bg2) confirms the cleanup class: the intended objects are the solid rectangular foreground components; remove isolated non-background pixels and fill/repair each object to its full rectangle using its dominant color. In the demo, the 1 rectangle at rows 2–5, cols 2–7 had intrusion 7 and stray 6, repaired to all 1; the 9 rectangle rows 3–7, cols 13–15 had intrusions 6/3, repaired to all 9; the 5 rectangle rows 8–9, cols 7–9 had an intrusion removed and empty interior cells filled; the 9 rectangle rows 11–15, cols 4–9 repaired intrusions 0/3/7; the 8 rectangle rows 24–26, cols 11–13 repaired to full 3x3. Small 1 object at rows 13–14, cols 12–13 was preserved. The isolated noise of colors 0,3,6,7 was erased. The test was solved by removing isolated 4 and 9, and filling the 7 rectangles: top r0–6,c10–14, and middle r9–13,c5–11; background 1 preserved. Confirmed by accepted submission.

Important refinement: components can be separated by background and have different dimensions; detect foreground rectangular regions and restore the rectangle's dominant color, while deleting isolated speckles. Avoid broadening or merging neighboring components.

## Confirmed additional recurrence (accepted after 3 wrong submissions)

This test input was 14x21, background 4. The accepted output preserved the principal colored regions and cleaned the sparse foreign-color noise: completed/regularized the two upper motifs (color 1 block at rows 0-1, cols 3-6; color 0 block rows 3-4, cols 0-3; color 5 block rows 1-3, cols 14-16), cleared stray markers outside these objects (including 7, 2, 8, 9), and retained the lower color-0 structured areas/rectangles (including columns 9-10 and 13-14 in rows 6-12, plus color-0 region rows 9-12 cols 16-19 and bottom row 13 cols 16-19). The successful output repairs embedded foreign cells within selected shapes and removes external singleton noise. Importantly, this recurrence confirms that the object-cleanup family can include both complete solid rectangles and multi-part shapes; previous generic rectangle/singleton hypotheses had failed in other recurrences and must not be treated as universally sufficient. Do not assume every apparent rectangle is repaired or every foreign singleton erased: compare the selection and shape boundaries in demos. This exact run's accepted transformation is evidence for this family, not a universal cellwise formula absent an exact selector.

## Confirmed rule from this recurrence (accepted test)
Task operation: Preserve only the broad, solid foreground rectangular objects (and any pre-existing structured multi-cell objects); erase scattered isolated foreground noise. Crucial distinction: do NOT complete/fill all apparent regions or blobs. The relevant rectangles are those that are internally filled as compact blocks, while noisy isolated markers and small local intrusions are removed. In the test (29x21, bg2), accepted output erased every singleton noise and removed marker-color 6 cells intruding in the small 0 block at rows 7-9, cols 4-6, leaving that block as its original 3x3 all-0 rectangle; similarly removed isolated 8/6 etc. Preserved the 9 block rows 6-9, cols 12-18 as 9 (corrected its intrusions); preserved the 5 rectangle rows 16-20, cols 5-8; preserved the left 9 rectangle rows 18-21, cols 0-2; preserved the bottom-left 0 object rows 23-28, cols 4-9, including its foreign 4/6 intrusions repaired to 0; and preserved the small bottom-right 0 rectangle rows 23-26, cols 12-13. Importantly, the correct output retained the two large 0 rectangles at bottom, which the earlier failed predictions had incorrectly deleted, and kept the 5 block; the transformation is targeted cleanup/repair, not wholesale recoloring or just singleton deletion.

Demo evidence for this recurrence: Pair 1 (bg7) repaired two distinct 0 rectangles (rows 0-6, col6-7; rows1-3, cols10-13) and retained 9 rectangle at rows7-8 cols0-4, 8 objects in lower right; cleaned external isolated noise and repaired foreign intrusions. Pair 2 (bg5) removed sparse noise while preserving rectangular 3 objects at rows0-7 cols1-7, 4 blocks at rows1-3 cols10-12 and rows14-17 (two adjacent blocks separated by a column), 2 block rows10-12 cols7-10, and 2 block rows20-21 cols0-1; corrected intrusions. Pair 3 (bg0) only corrected one intrusion in 9 rectangle rows4-9 cols2-6; other background unchanged. Pair 4 (bg9) repaired several 1,6,3,2 blocks and removed sparse noise; preserved object footprints including blocks. Combined with accepted test, the cleanup scope includes solid rectangular objects of multiple colors/dimensions, removes isolated noise, and repairs embedded foreign-color cells to object color; avoid assuming every apparent component gets expanded, and preserve object boundaries exactly.

Operational rule now supported by demos/test: identify foreground rectangular object footprints from repeated/dense regions; for each selected rectangle, restore all its cells to its dominant foreground color. Remove external non-background singletons. Do not extend boundaries, merge neighboring objects, or erase valid rectangles. In tests with ambiguity, request a demo rather than broad deletion: earlier submissions based on removing noise plus filling all candidate shapes, and clearing most of the grid except a few suspected major objects, were rejected.

## Recurrence workflow

Always return one protocol-compliant JSON action only.
1. Load this skill, then extract exact input/output cell differences for every new demo.
2. Separate singleton removal, within-object intrusion repair, and object selection as distinct decisions. Look for color/shape/relative-position constraints beyond component size.
3. Record unchanged singleton-like or multi-cell counterparts as negative evidence.
4. Require a candidate to reproduce every demo cell by cell before applying it.
5. Do not reuse any prior failed guess or accepted test output as a template; this is a task-family reminder, not a solved formula.
6. Return one protocol-compliant JSON action only.
